props.title: Nine Queens
props.initialSlug: Two con men, one mark, endless twists

sections.content: Nine Queens revolutionized the con artist thriller genre with its labyrinthine Argentine swagger. Director Fabián Bielinsky crafts a masterclass in misdirection that influenced films like The Italian Job (2003) and Focus (2015). The film follows two small-time swindlers who stumble into an elaborate stamp collection scam during Argentina's economic crisis. Like House of Games (1987), it delights in showing the mechanics of street cons before pulling the rug out with bigger deceptions.

sections.content: What sets Nine Queens apart is how it weaves Argentina's 2001 economic collapse into its fabric of deception. The film's atmosphere of financial desperation and institutional distrust creates perfect conditions for con artists to thrive. This social commentary through genre lens approach influenced later films like Parasite (2019) and Bad Education (2019), where systemic corruption enables individual scams.

The film's influence extends to the wave of international con artist thrillers that followed, including Confidence (2003) and Criminal (2004), which was an American remake. Like The Spanish Prisoner (1997), it demonstrates how the con game format can transcend cultural boundaries while maintaining local specificity. SUBHEAD: The Art of the Long Con

sections.content: Nine Queens excels at showing the psychology of the con, particularly through the mentor-protégé relationship between Marcos and Juan. This dynamic echoes through films like American Hustle (2013) and Catch Me If You Can (2002), where the thrill of the con becomes addictive and moral lines blur. The film's exploration of trust and betrayal between con artists themselves became a template for later entries in the genre.
